newsitem.title: UK: UBS sees cautious UK budget, 2 bln stg tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: UBS sees cautious UK budget, 2 bln stg tax cuts.

text.p: Economists at UBS forecast that British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke will unveil a cautious budget on November 26, with net tax reductions of just two billion stg.

"Our over-riding assumption is that the chancellor will put all his eggs in one basket -- namely a highly visible, headline-grabbing reduction in the basic rate of personal income tax, coupled with increases in the lower rate tax band and personal allowances," they wrote in their budget preview.
UBS said Clarke would want to avoid the inevitable adverse financial market reaction which would follow large net tax cuts.
"This reaction would necessitate a tightening of monetary policy, destroying any political capital gained from his decision to reduce taxation."

Clarke would also want to show that the public finances were on course to meet the Maastricht criteria and that they were on a sustainable footing in the medium term. Among measures to offset the loss of revenue, UBS said Clarke might reduce the tax relief on profit-related pay, but he is unlikely to abolish it outright as this would hit many Conservative voters.
UBS said the gilts market would take net tax cuts of two to three billion stg in its stride. "Risks are asymmetrically skewed in favour of gilt outperformance post-budget," it said.

Equities are also broadly discounting a tax giveaway in this range and a giveaway of up to five billion stg is "unlikely to significantly change forecasts of company earnings/dividend growth in 1997." Other points from the UBS budget preview included:
- annual exemptions from capital gains tax are likely to be increased but outright abolition is unlikely this year;
- the threshold for inheritance tax may be increased;
- no change is seen in either employee or employer national insurance contributions;
- no change is expected in either the rate or extent of value-added tax, although spending on the national lottery could be taxed at a higher rate;
- the Chancellor is likely to stick to the practice of increasing road fuel duties by at least five percent plus inflation and to raise most tobacco duties by at least three percent in real terms;
- alcohol duties are expected to rise in line with inflation, although a doubling of the duty on "alco-pop" is a possibility;
- insurance premium tax could be increased by two percentage points, raising around 600 million stg in revenue;
- the corporate sector looks relatively safe from tax increases.
